title: External audit log egress and customer-managed storage bindings for Private/VPC deployments
creator: Riley Chen
description:
Summary:
Provide a robust, secure, and configurable mechanism for forwarding audit logs out of Private/VPC/on‑prem Redwood deployments into customer‑managed storage or collectors. This feature supports regulatory compliance and enterprise requirements for log custody and KMS control while preserving Redwood’s reliability and observability for operations teams.

Goals:
- Allow customers to store audit logs in their own storage endpoints (S3/GCS/Azure Blob or on‑prem SIEM/collector) under customer control (cross-account role or mutually authenticated endpoint).
- Support both push and pull delivery modes for different network topologies and offline/on‑prem constraints.
- Preserve integrity and non‑repudiation: sign/upload batches, include sequence IDs and checksums.
- Provide per‑tenant configuration guarded by RBAC v2 and admin approval flows (SSO/SAML).
- Minimal performance impact on runtime; durable, encrypted local buffering for backpressure and retry.

Non-goals:
- Building a long‑term ingestion pipeline for arbitrary third‑party analytics (we expose structured exports and connectors instead).
- Replacing customer SIEMs – we integrate via standard protocols.

Requirements (functional):
- Support S3-compatible endpoints (AWS S3, MinIO, Ceph) with two auth modes: cross-account IAM role assumption and presigned PUTs.
- Support GCS/Azure via signed URLs or service account impersonation.
- Support on‑prem collectors over mutual‑TLS HTTPS and syslog (rfc5424) with TLS.
- Allow per‑tenant retention and export filters (audit events scope).
- Admin UI + API for configuring egress targets, with RBAC enforcement (only admin roles may create/modify bindings).
- Plumb audit trail for egress configuration changes into Redwood control-plane audit (with option to forward those records as well).

Requirements (non‑functional):
- At‑least‑once delivery with idempotent consumers; document ordering guarantees.
- Local buffering encrypted with customer CMK where available; otherwise encrypted with platform key but flagged.
- End‑to‑end TLS with certificate pinning for critical endpoints.
- Retry/backoff policy with dead‑letter queue option for failed deliveries.
- Metrics and alerting: delivery latency, queue size, failure rate, last successful write per target.

Design options considered (high level):
1) Cross‑Account Write (recommended for cloud object stores): Redwood assumes a customer IAM role/impersonates GCP service account and writes directly into customer bucket. Pros: efficient, server‑side encryption with customer KMS possible, direct custody. Cons: requires cloud IAM configuration by customer; not always possible for air‑gapped on‑prem installs.

2) Presigned Uploads (push using short‑lived signed URLs): Redwood generates presigned PUT URLs and pushes batches. Pros: simpler permissions, no permanent role to configure. Cons: slightly more complex when rotation and large volumes; trust boundary around signing process.

3) Customer Collector (pull from/redwood push to on‑prem collector via mTLS): Redwood opens outbound HTTPS/TCP to customer collector endpoint using mutual TLS and delivers events in NDJSON batches. Pros: supports air‑gapped topologies via reverse proxy; integrates with SIEMs. Cons: requires customer to manage collector availability; must handle firewalls.

4) Local Replication + Cross‑account Sync: For strict air‑gapped installs we provide a lightweight on‑prem agent that writes to a local mount and the customer’s replication process moves data offsite. Pros: minimal network changes; customer remains in control of pipeline. Cons: places more operational burden on customer.

Tradeoffs and chosen approach:
- We will support (1) Cross‑Account Write and (3) Customer Collector as primary delivery modes for 80%+ of use cases, offering Presigned Uploads as an alternative for customers refusing cross‑account roles. The local replication mode is supported as a documented pattern and an optional agent for Private installs (opt‑in).
- Integrity: all batches will be signed by a deployment‑scoped key. Signatures and checksums are embedded as metadata on the objects or as companion .sig files. This enables customer verification and tamper detection.

Proposed architecture (component flow):
- Source: Audit event stream (control plane + data plane events) -> normalizer -> batching window (configurable size/time) -> signer -> local durable queue (encrypted) -> delivery workers (per target) -> target (S3/GCS/collector).
- Durable queue: lightweight RocksDB-backed queue or append file in /var/lib/redwood/auditqueue encrypted with KMS; rotation to disk with size thresholds.
- Delivery semantics: at‑least‑once with idempotency keys per batched chunk (UUID + start_ts + end_ts). Consumers/storage writes should be idempotent by object key (key includes stable tenant + chunk id).
- Observability: a per‑target telemetry stream and dashboard; logs for delivery attempts, latency, errors, and last successful sequence ID.

Config API and sample YAML (as string example for each tenant):
api_version: redwood.audit/v1
kind: AuditEgressBinding
metadata:
  tenant_id: t-12345
  name: legal-compliance-eu
spec:
  mode: s3
  s3_config:
    bucket: "customer-audit-bucket"
    path_prefix: "redwood/tenants/t-12345/"
    auth: cross_account_role
    role_arn: "arn:aws:iam::012345678901:role/RedwoodAuditWriter"
    kms_key_arn: "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:012345678901:key/abcd-..."
  filters:
    include: ["admin.*","auth.*"]
  retention_days: "365"
  encryption_policy: "customer-cmk"
  verify_signatures: "true"
  notifications:
    on_failure: "pagerduty://SVC-REDWOOD-AUDIT"

RBAC and admin controls:
- RBAC v2 will introduce a new resource type AuditEgressBinding. Actions: create/read/update/delete are limited to users with the admin audit role.
- Any create/update operation triggers an SSO/SAML admin approval flow for enterprise accounts with policy: "Require 2 administrators from different groups to approve outbound log egress to external locations." Approval events are logged in our internal audit store and optionally forwarded.
- UI: console shows egress bindings with validation status, last delivery timestamp, and a test delivery button that performs a one‑off signed upload.

Security considerations and hardening:
- Key management: prefer customer‑managed KMS for encrypting on‑disk buffers and object server‑side encryption. If customer KMS is not available, platform encryption is used but flagged to customer and security team.
- Mutual TLS: for on‑prem collectors require client certificate issued by customer CA; Redwood will support CA pinning and rotation APIs.
- Least privilege: when assuming roles, use narrowly scoped policies (PutObject, PutObjectAcl limited to prefix).
- Tamper evidence: sign every chunk with deployment key; option to publish public signing keys for customers to verify.
- Privacy: redact PII per tenant configuration before forwarding if requested.

Reliability, backpressure, and failover:
- Queue thresholds trigger health signals that can slow non‑critical telemetry to protect audit delivery.
- On persistent failure to deliver, events can be moved to a dead‑letter bucket (configurable retention) and an alert raised.
- Canary/rollout: feature flag gating by deployment, start with 2 internal customers and 3 private deployments, then 10% rollout across private fleet.

Testing and validation plan:
- Integration tests with test S3 bucket (cross‑account role) and a local MinIO cluster; simulate KMS rotation and 10x normal write load.
- On‑prem test harness: local collector that accepts mTLS and validates signatures and ordering.
- Chaos tests: kill delivery worker, simulate network partitions, ensure at‑least‑once and reordering handling.
- Compliance checks: verify retention, deletion flow, and admin approval audit trail.

Migration and rollout steps:
1) Build control plane API and RBAC resource types (ENG-25713 core).
2) Implement S3 cross‑account and presigned flows; internal tests.
3) Add mTLS collector client and syslog adapter.
4) Add encrypted local queue and signing.
5) Canaries + partner testing with 2 customers.
6) Full rollout and deprecation of any legacy ad‑hoc forwarding endpoints.

Operational metrics and SLOs:
- Delivery success rate >= 99.9% over 30 days (for cloud targets).
- Median delivery latency <= 30s for targets in same region.
- Alert if queue growth > 95th percentile or any target fails 3 consecutive deliveries.

Open questions / decisions required:
- Do we require a mandatory customer KMS for disk encryption in Private installs, or allow platform fallback with explicit acceptance?
- Which exact approval policy to bake into the SSO flow (2 admin requirement vs configurable per org)?
- Define canonical key rotation process for signing keys and customer notification timeline.

Deliverables:
- API spec (OpenAPI YAML), Console UI screens, RBAC policy docs, operator runbook, integration tests, and an example on‑prem collector image.
